title: What are you doing?
goal: Use present-tense verbs — the main engine of Hebrew — and place אֶת, the object marker with no English equivalent at all.
bekal: build sentences with verbs in all four forms
put אֶת in the right place

dialogs.title: שִׂיחָה — בַּסִּפְרִיָּה
dialogs.intro: Budi runs into Dana at the library one afternoon.

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: Budi! What are you doing here?

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: I'm writing a paper for university.

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: About the history of Tel Aviv.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: אַתְּ קוֹרֵאת אֶת כָּל הַסְּפָרִים הָאֵלֶּה?
lines.baca: at koret et kol hasfarim ha'eleh?
lines.id: Are you reading all these books?

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.text: לֹא הַכֹּל. אֲנִי קוֹרֵאת רַק שְׁנֵי פְּרָקִים.
lines.baca: lo hakol. ani koret rak shnei prakim.
lines.id: Not all of them. I've only read two chapters.
lines.literal: not all. I read (f) only two chapters.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: אֲנִי לֹא מֵבִין אֶת הַמִּלָּה הַזֹּאת.
lines.baca: ani lo mevin et hamilah hazot.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: הַמִּלָּה הַזֹּאת. אֲנִי מְחַפֵּשׂ אוֹתָהּ בַּמִּלּוֹן.
lines.baca: hamilah hazot. ani mekhapes otah bamilon.
lines.id: This word. I'm looking it up in the dictionary.
lines.literal: the-word the-this. I look-for her in-the-dictionary.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: תּוֹדָה! אַתְּ מַסְבִּירָה יוֹתֵר טוֹב מֵהַמִּלּוֹן.
lines.baca: todah! at masbirah yoter tov mehamilon.
lines.id: Thanks! You explain better than the dictionary.
lines.literal: thanks! you (f) explain more good from-the-dictionary.

notes: ⚠️ **This is the big load of this unit: present-tense verbs change according to who does the action.** אֲנִי לוֹמֵד if you're a man, אֲנִי לוֹמֶדֶת if you're a woman. English never asks this of you — "I study" is "I study", whoever you are.
**The good news: it isn't the person that matters, only gender & number.** So אֲנִי, אַתָּה, and הוּא all use **exactly the same** form (לוֹמֵד). You need only four forms for everyone, not six.

**The Hebrew present covers two English tenses at once.** אֲנִי לוֹמֵד means "I study" (habit) **and** "I'm studying" (right now). Hebrew doesn't distinguish them — one form, two meanings, and context decides.

⚠️ **אֶת is a word that means nothing**, and that's exactly why learners forget it. It goes in front of a **definite** object: one with הַ־, a proper name, or a pronoun. אֲנִי קוֹרֵאת סֵפֶר (no אֶת — any book) but אֲנִי קוֹרֵאת אֶת הַסֵּפֶר (with אֶת — the book).
**Quick self-check:** if your English has "the", "this", a name, or him/her/it as the object, you need אֶת. "I'm reading a book" → no אֶת. "I'm reading the book" → with אֶת.
**עַל** (*al*) means "about" **and** "on". עַל מָה אַתְּ כּוֹתֶבֶת? = what are you writing about?; הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן = the book is on the table. Context tells them apart.

**אוֹתָהּ** in line 10 is "her/it" as an object: אֶת + she. The full set (אוֹתִי, אוֹתְךָ, אוֹתוֹ, אוֹתָהּ …) is in the second box — and once again, it's just אֶת taking endings, the same machinery as שֶׁל in unit 4.
**יוֹתֵר טוֹב מִ־** = "better than". The pattern: יוֹתֵר + adjective + מִ. Full comparisons come in unit 13, but you can use this one now.

grammars.title: Present-tense verbs: one pattern, four forms
body: The biggest verb group (called פָּעַל, *pa'al*) uses this pattern. Once you see it, hundreds of verbs open up at once.
after: Notice the **וֹ** that always appears after the first root letter — that's the signature of the pa'al present. Whenever you see the pattern ־וֹ־ֵ־ in Hebrew text, you know it's a verb in the present.

⚠️ Verbs whose last root letter is **ה** deviate a little: עוֹשֶׂה / עוֹשָׂה / עוֹשִׂים / עוֹשׂוֹת (do), רוֹצֶה / רוֹצָה / רוֹצִים / רוֹצוֹת (want), קוֹנֶה (buy), שׁוֹתֶה (drink). The feminine is ־ָה, not ־ֶת. A small group, but full of the most common words.

grammars.title: אֶת with endings: "I see him"
body: When the object is a pronoun, אֶת fuses with it into one word. Same machinery as שֶׁל.

Example
rows: הוּא רוֹאֶה אוֹתִי — he sees me
אֲנִי מַכִּיר אוֹתְךָ — I know you
אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אוֹתָהּ — I love her
הֵם מְחַכִּים לָנוּ — they're waiting for us
אֲנִי רוֹאֶה אֶתְכֶם — I see you all
אֲנִי מַכִּיר אוֹתָם — I know them

after: English already has object pronouns (me, him, her), but Hebrew splits further: "you" and "them" each come in masculine and feminine. Practice the three most common first: אוֹתִי, אוֹתוֹ, אוֹתָהּ.

sections.title: Twenty verbs that cover everyday conversation

blocks.text: ⚠️ Verbs ending in a throat letter (ע, ח) take ־ַ־ַת in the feminine: שׁוֹמַעַת, יוֹדַעַת, לוֹקַחַת. It looks like an exception, but it's just a sound adjustment — throat letters pull the vowel toward *a*.

**מְדַבֵּר** and **מְחַפֵּשׂ** start with מְ, not וֹ. They belong to another verb family (called פִּעֵל, *pi'el*) with the pattern מְ־ַ־ֵ־. Just note it for now: if a verb starts with מְ, its feminine also ends in ־ֶת.

blocks.title: Three lifesaver sentences for learners
items: **אֲנִי לֹא מֵבִין / מְבִינָה** — I don't understand. Don't be shy; it's the most useful sentence in the whole course.
**אֵיךְ אוֹמְרִים "table" בְּעִבְרִית?** — how to grow your vocabulary straight from conversation, no dictionary needed.
**מָה זֶה אוֹמֵר?** — what does it mean? Literally "what does this say?", and Israelis use it exactly that way.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of the verb.
Add אֶת where needed; where it isn't, write a dash.

items: How do you say "door" in Hebrew?

answers: לוֹמֶדֶת — עוֹבְדִים — קוֹרֵא — שׁוֹתוֹת — מְבִינָה — מְשַׂחֲקִים
הִיא כּוֹתֶבֶת מִכְתָּב. — אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדַעַת. — הִיא שׁוֹמַעַת מוּזִיקָה. — הֵן עוֹשׂוֹת שִׁעוּרִים.
אֲנִי כּוֹתֶבֶת מִכְתָּב. — אַתָּה מֵבִין אֶת הַמִּלָּה הַזֹּאת? — הֵם עוֹבְדִים בְּחֵיפָה. — אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ. — אֵיךְ אוֹמְרִים "door" בְּעִבְרִית?
wave: All day tomorrow, every time you do something, say it in your head: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ, אֲנִי קוֹרֵא. Make sure the form matches your own gender.
